plants.name: Aster novi-belgii
plants.description: A clump-forming perennial with abundant daisy-like flower heads featuring yellow centers surrounded by narrow petal-like rays. It is a vital late-season nectar source for bees and migrating monarch butterflies.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer to autumn (August to October)
plants.location: Eastern North America, widely cultivated in temperate gardens worldwide
plants.funFact: The name Aster comes from the Greek word for star, and the flowers are a key fuel stop for monarch butterflies on their autumn migration to Mexico.

plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: A bulbous perennial whose goblet-shaped flowers emerge naked from the ground in autumn, without leaves, which appear the following spring. Often seen in damp meadows and woodland edges.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer to autumn (September to October)
plants.location: Europe, from Britain and Ireland to the Balkans; cultivated in temperate gardens
plants.funFact: Despite its name it is not a true crocus, and all parts are highly toxic because they contain colchicine, a compound used in medicine to treat gout.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.description: A small evergreen tree or large shrub with feathery blue-green foliage and fragrant, fluffy golden globular flower clusters that light up the Australian bush as winter turns to spring.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late winter to spring in the Southern Hemisphere (July to October)
plants.location: Southeastern Australia, including Victoria, South Australia and New South Wales
plants.funFact: Golden Wattle is Australia's national floral emblem, and National Wattle Day is celebrated on September 1, the first day of spring.

plants.name: Helianthus annuus
plants.description: A tall annual with large bright flower heads that track the sun when young. In September, late plantings and fields are in full bloom or setting seed, attracting bees, finches and other wildlife.
plants.bloomingSeason: Summer to early autumn (July to September)
plants.location: Native to North America; cultivated across Europe, Russia, Ukraine, Argentina and temperate regions worldwide
plants.funFact: Young sunflower buds follow the sun from east to west in a behavior called heliotropism, but mature flowers stay facing east.
